performers: Constance Schoepflin, flute; Advent Chamber Orchestra
intro: Constance Schoepflin and the Advent Chamber Orchestra play the quick finale of Bach’s G major Flute Concerto. The flute starts among the strings, then breaks away with trills and long runs of its own.

sections.label: A · Flute and strings together
sections.mNote: The whole ensemble shares the opening G major tune

sections.label: B · The flute takes its solo
sections.mNote: An added trill and slur reshape the opening tune

sections.label: C · Flute runs and string replies
sections.mNote: Long solo phrases alternate with shorter orchestral answers

sections.label: D · A fermata over D
sections.mNote: The flute holds G above the bass’s D

sections.label: E · The opening tune resumes
sections.mNote: Flute and strings recover the rising figure

sections.label: A′ · The ensemble closes in G
sections.mNote: Flute joins strings and bass for the final tutti

cues.title: A tune for everyone
cues.text: The Presto begins with a little rising scale, clipped notes and a trill. Flute and strings share the tune; the bass has running notes of its own. Quick switches between piano and forte give the opening a mischievous edge.
cues.evidence: Critical performing parts, flute and basso, Presto bars 1–48, PDF pp. 21–22. https://cpebach.org/pdfs/parts/Wq169-flute-parts.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The flute adds a trill
cues.text: For its first solo, the flute takes the opening tune and gives it a new flourish: a trill on the pickup G and a slur across the bar line. The strings step back into accompaniment. The same rising notes acquire a more supple voice.
cues.evidence: First solo at bar 49, critical flute part, PDF p. 22. Kuijken discusses the added trill and slur in the edition’s introduction. https://cpebach.org/pdfs/parts/Wq169-flute-parts.pdf ; https://cpebach.org/pdfs/introductions/III-FS-Wq169-Intro.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An organ concerto finds breath
cues.text: Bach first writes this concerto for organ in 1755. To make a flute version, he raises low passages, changes others and leaves room for breathing. A keyboard player’s hands can keep going when a flautist’s lungs cannot.
cues.evidence: Barthold Kuijken, introduction to Wq 169: organ original Wq 34, dated 1755; flute adaptation made before 1768, with changes to range and breathing. https://cpebach.org/pdfs/introductions/III-FS-Wq169-Intro.pdf

cues.title: At Frederick’s keyboard
cues.text: In 1740 Bach accompanies Frederick II’s first flute solo after his accession, at Charlottenburg. The king’s new harpsichordist is twenty-six. Flute playing is part of his daily professional world at the Prussian court.
cues.evidence: Bach’s autobiographical account, quoted in The Essential C. P. E. Bach, introduction, p. xviii; the court appointment begins in 1740. https://www.cpebach.org/pdfs/introductions/Essential-CPEB-Intro.pdf

cues.title: A blank staff for Bach
cues.text: A copyist writes out the keyboard concerto and leaves the top staff empty. Bach fills it with a flute part in his own hand, then changes the accompaniment. The surviving manuscript catches the composer at work, turning one solo instrument’s music into another’s.
cues.evidence: Kuijken identifies copyist Anon. 303 and Bach’s autograph additions in Berlin manuscript Mus. ms. Bach P 769. https://cpebach.org/pdfs/introductions/III-FS-Wq169-Intro.pdf

cues.title: G hangs over D
cues.text: The running flute line reaches a fermata: G hangs above D in the bass. The violins and viola rest. Bach writes a little turn and the descent towards the returning tune after this held point; the breathless movement has made room for a breath.
cues.evidence: Presto bar 236 and return at 237: flute, PDF p. 27; resting upper strings, pp. 42, 56 and 69; basso fermata, p. 84. https://cpebach.org/pdfs/parts/Wq169-flute-parts.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Three bars for the lungs
cues.text: Late in the finale, Bach inserts three bars absent from the organ version. The flute rests while the strings play. Then the soloist starts another long run. The new bars give a human breath to a phrase first imagined for a keyboard.
cues.evidence: Kuijken identifies the inserted orchestral intervention at Presto bars 287–89 as a breathing opportunity. This note concerns the adaptation, not a timed entry. https://cpebach.org/pdfs/introductions/III-FS-Wq169-Intro.pdf

cues.title: The flute rejoins the strings
cues.text: The final tutti brings the flute back into the ensemble’s tune. Trills, slurred pairs and repeated high notes lead towards the close. Flute, strings and bass arrive together on G major.
cues.evidence: Closing tutti, bars 314–335: flute, PDF p. 29; first violin, p. 43; basso, p. 85. https://cpebach.org/pdfs/parts/Wq169-flute-parts.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A trill makes the tune solo
transitions.to: B · The flute takes its solo
transitions.how: The opening ensemble passage closes in G major. The flute takes the rising theme alone, adding a trill to the pickup G and slurring across the bar line. Strings and bass accompany more quietly beneath it. The tempo stays Presto; the extra ornament and changed balance distinguish the solo.
transitions.evidence: Presto bars 47–50, critical flute part, PDF p. 22; Kuijken’s introduction discusses the solo ornament. https://cpebach.org/pdfs/parts/Wq169-flute-parts.pdf ; https://cpebach.org/pdfs/introductions/III-FS-Wq169-Intro.pdf

transitions.title: The run stops over D
transitions.from: C · Flute runs and string replies
transitions.how: Descending flute semiquavers run above repeated D notes in the bass. They stop at a fermata, with G in the flute suspended above the bass’s held D. The violins and viola are silent. The figured bass marks the suspended fourth resolving to a third before the G major theme returns.
transitions.evidence: Presto bars 233–237: flute and figured bass, PDF p. 27; upper-string rests, pp. 42, 56 and 69; basso, p. 84. https://cpebach.org/pdfs/parts/Wq169-flute-parts.pdf

transitions.title: The ensemble answers the fermata
transitions.how: After the held D in the bass, a low G announces the return. The flute’s pickup leads into the opening scale, now shared with the violins. Viola and bass resume their moving parts under the forte ensemble. The music keeps its two-four metre and Presto pace.
transitions.evidence: Presto bars 236–240, flute, PDF p. 27; first violin, p. 42; viola, p. 69; basso, p. 84. https://cpebach.org/pdfs/parts/Wq169-flute-parts.pdf

transitions.title: All together for the last cadence
transitions.to: A′ · The ensemble closes in G
transitions.how: The solo flute’s running line gives way to a shared tutti, marked forte in the strings and bass. Slurred pairs and repeated high notes recall the opening. The bass works through the closing phrases to a final D–G cadence, with the flute joining the strings on the G major ending.
transitions.evidence: Presto bars 314–335: flute, PDF p. 29; first violin, p. 43; basso, p. 85. https://cpebach.org/pdfs/parts/Wq169-flute-parts.pdf

source.title: C. P. E. Bach, flute-concerto working score, Mus. ms. Bach P 769
source.locator: Presto, manuscript PDF pp. 11–39. Critical performing parts supply the flute’s ensemble passages: https://cpebach.org/pdfs/parts/Wq169-flute-parts.pdf, pp. 21–29. The fermata and string rests appear on pp. 27, 42, 56, 69 and 84. The cello desk represents the written basso part.

timeline.note: Flute joins the strings and bass in the opening tune, with quick piano and forte replies.
The flute adds a trill and slur to the opening theme; strings and bass accompany its first solo.
Long flute runs alternate with shorter string phrases above the moving bass.
At the fermata, the flute holds G above D in the bass. Violins and viola rest.
Flute and violins recover the opening rising figure, with viola and bass moving below them.
The closing tutti joins flute, strings and bass in the final G major cadence.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Flute version of the concerto; complete finale only
fields.note: Only movement III is hosted in this package. Set metadata records part 3 of 3, not possession of the preceding Allegro di molto and Largo. The 1755 date belongs to the original organ concerto Wq 34; the flute adaptation is later and cannot be assigned a precise year. The working manuscript is dated between 1755 and 1768 by Kuijken. The recording’s performing edition, any restored missing bar and the details of a cadenza are unestablished. The modern critical performing parts clarify the manuscript’s shorthand: flute participates in the opening and closing tutti, so a blank flute staff does not establish a rest. These parts are consulted as a reference, not attributed to the 2008 performance or claimed to be public domain. The score-derived orchestra display uses passage overviews rather than aligned entries; the cello desk represents written basso, not a verified allocation of bass instruments.

composer.epithet: Frederick the Great’s accompanist wrote keyboard music that breaks off mid-sentence and makes a single note tremble.
facts: His father, Johann Sebastian Bach; studied law in Leipzig and Frankfurt an der Oder
Frederick II’s harpsichordist, 1740–67 · Hamburg music director, 1768–88
Essay on the True Art of Playing Keyboard Instruments, 1753 and 1762
Wq: Alfred Wotquenne · H: E. Eugene Helm

quote.text: A musician can move others only if he is moved himself.
quote.source: Essay on the True Art of Playing Keyboard Instruments, Part I, chapter 3, §13 (1753); our translation

composer.background:
On 12 October 1772, Charles Burney went to dinner with Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach in Hamburg. Bach’s wife, his lawyer son, his daughter and three or four friends were there; upstairs was a music room hung with pictures, drawings and prints of more than a hundred and fifty musicians. Before dinner Bach had played his Silbermann clavichord; afterwards Burney talked him back to the keyboard, and he played almost until eleven. His eyes became fixed, his lower lip dropped, and Burney watched a sociable host disappear into his own music. On a long note, Burney wrote, Bach could draw from the clavichord “a cry of sorrow and complaint”.

Emanuel was born in Weimar on 8 March 1714, the second surviving son of Johann Sebastian Bach and Maria Barbara. Telemann was his godfather. The household moved to Cöthen in 1717 and Leipzig in 1723, when Sebastian became Thomaskantor. Visiting musicians came to play for his father; the boy heard them at home. “In composition and keyboard playing I never had any teacher other than my father,” he wrote in the autobiography published in 1773.
